claim: Mosquitoes are the top vectors for arthropod-borne diseases, being implicated in the transmission of many human pathogens responsible for arboviral diseases, malaria, and lymphatic filariasis.
source: Mosquitoes top the list of vectors for arthropod-borne diseases, being implicated in the transmission of many human pathogens responsible for arboviral diseases, malaria, and lymphatic filariasis (WHO, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2017.

claim: Mosquito-borne viruses circulate in sylvatic (between wild animals) or urban (between humans) transmission cycles driven by different mosquito species with their own distinct host preferences.
source: Mosquito-borne viruses circulate in sylvatic (between wild animals) or urban (between humans) transmission cycles driven by different mosquito species with their own distinct host preferences.
evidence: The claim draws from established scientific knowledge about mosquito-borne virus transmission patterns.

claim: Urban mosquito species are chiefly responsible for amplifying epidemics in dense human populations.
source: Although urban mosquito species are chiefly responsible for amplifying epidemics in dense human populations, sylvatic mosquitoes maintain the transmission of these viruses among forest-dwelling animal reservoir hosts and are involved in spillover events when humans enter their ecological niches (Valentine et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Valentine et al., 2019.

claim: Sylvatic mosquitoes maintain the transmission of viruses among forest-dwelling animal reservoir hosts and are involved in spillover events when humans enter their ecological niches.
source: Although urban mosquito species are chiefly responsible for amplifying epidemics in dense human populations, sylvatic mosquitoes maintain the transmission of these viruses among forest-dwelling animal reservoir hosts and are involved in spillover events when humans enter their ecological niches (Valentine et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Valentine et al., 2019.

claim: Mosquito-borne virus emergence is preceded by spillover events.
source: Given that mosquito-borne virus emergence is preceded by such spillover events, continuous surveillance and virus discovery in sylvatic mosquitoes is integral to designing effective public health measures to pre-empt or respond to mosquito-borne viral epidemics.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about disease emergence patterns.

claim: Continuous surveillance and virus discovery in sylvatic mosquitoes is integral to designing effective public health measures to pre-empt or respond to mosquito-borne viral epidemics.
source: Given that mosquito-borne virus emergence is preceded by such spillover events, continuous surveillance and virus discovery in sylvatic mosquitoes is integral to designing effective public health measures to pre-empt or respond to mosquito-borne viral epidemics.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the relationship between spillover events and epidemic prevention.

claim: Metagenomics on field specimens is a powerful method to understand mosquito-borne disease ecology through the One Health lens.
source: Metagenomics on field specimens is a powerful method in our toolkit to understand mosquito-borne disease ecology through the One Health lens (Webster et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Webster et al., 2016.

claim: Next-generation sequencing has become more accessible.
source: With next-generation sequencing becoming more accessible, such studies have provided unprecedented insights into the interfaces among mosquitoes, their environment, and their animal and human hosts.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about technological advancement in sequencing.

claim: Metagenomics studies have provided unprecedented insights into the interfaces among mosquitoes, their environment, and their animal and human hosts.
source: With next-generation sequencing becoming more accessible, such studies have provided unprecedented insights into the interfaces among mosquitoes, their environment, and their animal and human hosts.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about the impact of metagenomics studies.

claim: Mosquito-associated viruses are mostly RNA viruses.
source: As mosquito-associated viruses are mostly RNA viruses, RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) is especially informative for surveillance and virus discovery.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about mosquito-borne pathogens.

claim: RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) is especially informative for surveillance and virus discovery of mosquito-associated viruses.
source: As mosquito-associated viruses are mostly RNA viruses, RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) is especially informative for surveillance and virus discovery.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the RNA nature of mosquito-associated viruses.

claim: Ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) comprise at least 80% of the total cellular RNA population.
source: These non-coding RNA molecules comprise at least 80% of the total cellular RNA population (Gale and Crampton, 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gale and Crampton, 1989.

claim: Due to their length and abundance, rRNAs are a sink for precious next-generation sequencing reads, decreasing the sensitivity of pathogen detection unless depleted during library preparation.
source: Due to their length and their abundance, they are a sink for precious next-generation sequencing reads, decreasing the sensitivity of pathogen detection unless depleted during library preparation.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the impact of rRNA on sequencing efficiency.

claim: The most common rRNA depletion protocols require prior knowledge of rRNA sequences of the species of interest.
source: Yet the most common rRNA depletion protocols require prior knowledge of rRNA sequences of the species of interest as they involve hybridizing antisense oligos to the rRNA molecules prior to removal by ribonucleases (Fauver et al., 2019; Phelps et al., 2021) or by bead capture (Kukutla et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fauver et al., 2019; Phelps et al., 2021; and Kukutla et al., 2013.

claim: Reference sequences for rRNAs are limited to only a handful of species from three genera: Aedes, Culex, and Anopheles.
source: Presently, reference sequences for rRNAs are limited to only a handful of species from three genera: Aedes, Culex, and Anopheles (Ruzzante et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ruzzante et al., 2019.

claim: The lack of reliable rRNA depletion methods could deter mosquito metagenomics studies from expanding their sampling diversity, resulting in a gap in knowledge of mosquito vector ecology.
source: The lack of reliable rRNA depletion methods could deter mosquito metagenomics studies from expanding their sampling diversity, resulting in a gap in our knowledge of mosquito vector ecology.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the consequences of limited rRNA depletion methods.

claim: Species identification based on morphology is notoriously complicated for members of certain species subgroups, especially among Culex subgroups.
source: Second, species identification based on morphology is notoriously complicated for members of certain species subgroups. This is especially the case among Culex subgroups.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about taxonomic challenges in mosquito identification.

claim: Sister species of Culex are often sympatric and show at least some competence for a number of viruses, such as Japanese encephalitis virus, St Louis encephalitic virus, and Usutu virus.
source: Sister species are often sympatric and show at least some competence for a number of viruses, such as Japanese encephalitis virus, St Louis encephalitic virus, and Usutu virus (Nchoutpouen et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nchoutpouen et al., 2019.

claim: Sister species of Culex share many morphological traits but have distinct ecologies and host preferences.
source: Although they share many morphological traits, each of these species have distinct ecologies and host preferences, thus the challenge of correctly identifying vector species can affect epidemiological risk estimation for these diseases (Farajollahi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Farajollahi et al., 2011.

claim: The challenge of correctly identifying vector species can affect epidemiological risk estimation for mosquito-borne diseases.
source: Although they share many morphological traits, each of these species have distinct ecologies and host preferences, thus the challenge of correctly identifying vector species can affect epidemiological risk estimation for these diseases (Farajollahi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Farajollahi et al., 2011.

claim: DNA molecular markers are often employed to a limited degree of success to distinguish between sister species of Culex.
source: DNA molecular markers are often employed to a limited degree of success to distinguish between sister species (Batovska et al., 2017; Zittra et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Batovska et al., 2017 and Zittra et al., 2016.

claim: The study sought to determine the 28S and 18S rRNA sequences of a diverse set of Old and New World sylvatic mosquito species from four countries: Cambodia, the Central African Republic, Madagascar, and French Guiana.
source: To address the lack of full-length rRNA sequences in public databases, we sought to determine the 28S and 18S rRNA sequences of a diverse set of Old and New World sylvatic mosquito species from four countries representing three continents: Cambodia, the Central African Republic, Madagascar, and French Guiana.
evidence: The claim describes the study's objective and is directly stated in the text.

claim: Cambodia, the Central African Republic, Madagascar, and French Guiana contain high mosquito biodiversity due to their proximity to the equator.
source: These countries, due to their proximity to the equator, contain high mosquito biodiversity (Foley et al., 2007) and have had long histories of mosquito-borne virus circulation (Desdouits et al., 2015; Halstead, 2019; Héraud et al., 2022; Jacobi and Serie, 1972; Ratsitorahina et al., 2008; Saluzzo et al., 2017; Zeller et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Foley et al., 2007.

claim: Cambodia, the Central African Republic, Madagascar, and French Guiana have had long histories of mosquito-borne virus circulation.
source: These countries, due to their proximity to the equator, contain high mosquito biodiversity (Foley et al., 2007) and have had long histories of mosquito-borne virus circulation (Desdouits et al., 2015; Halstead, 2019; Héraud et al., 2022; Jacobi and Serie, 1972; Ratsitorahina et al., 2008; Saluzzo et al., 2017; Zeller et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to Desdouits et al., 2015; Halstead, 2019; Héraud et al., 2022; Jacobi and Serie, 1972; Ratsitorahina et al., 2008; Saluzzo et al., 2017; Zeller et al., 2016.

claim: The study produced a dataset of 234 novel full-length 28S and 18S rRNA sequences from 33 mosquito species, 30 of which have never been recorded before.
source: Using a unique score-based read filtration strategy to remove interfering non-mosquito rRNA reads for accurate de novo assembly, we produced a dataset of 234 novel full-length 28S and 18S rRNA sequences from 33 mosquito species, 30 of which have never been recorded before.
evidence: The claim is supported by data generated in the study.

claim: The COI gene is the most widely used DNA marker for molecular species identification and forms the basis of the Barcode of Life Data System (BOLD).
source: The COI gene is the most widely used DNA marker for molecular species identification and forms the basis of the Barcode of Life Data System (BOLD) (Hebert et al., 2003; Ratnasingham and Hebert, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hebert et al., 2003 and Ratnasingham and Hebert, 2007.

claim: Full-length rRNA sequences are much less represented compared to other molecular markers.
source: Presently, full-length rRNA sequences are much less represented compared to other molecular markers.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about the state of molecular marker databases.

claim: Given the availability of relevant reference sequences, 28S and concatenated 28S+18S rRNA sequences can be the better approach for molecular taxonomy and phylogenetic studies.
source: However, given the availability of relevant reference sequences, 28S and concatenated 28S+18S rRNA sequences can be the better approach for molecular taxonomy and phylogenetic studies.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the potential utility of rRNA sequences.

claim: Using probes designed for the Ae. aegypti rRNA sequence followed by RNase H digestion produced poor depletion in Aedes albopictus, and in Culicine and Anopheline species, with between 46% and 94% of reads post-depletion being ribosomal.
source: In our hands, we have found that using probes designed for the Ae. aegypti rRNA sequence followed by RNase H digestion according to the protocol published by Morlan et al., 2012, produced poor depletion in Aedes albopictus, and in Culicine and Anopheline species (Figure 1), in which between 46% and 94% of reads post-depletion were ribosomal.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The lack of full-length reference rRNA sequences compromises the in silico clean-up of remaining rRNA reads from sequencing data, as reads belonging to variable regions would not be removed.
source: Additionally, the lack of full-length reference rRNA sequences compromises the in silico clean-up of remaining rRNA reads from sequencing data, as reads belonging to variable regions would not be removed.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the limitations of incomplete reference sequences.

claim: The study performed RNA-seq to generate reference rRNA sequences for 33 mosquito species representing 10 genera from Cambodia, the Central African Republic, Madagascar, and French Guiana.
source: To solve this and to enable RNA-seq metagenomics on a broader range of mosquito species, we performed RNA-seq to generate reference rRNA sequences for 33 mosquito species representing 10 genera from Cambodia, the Central African Republic, Madagascar, and French Guiana.
evidence: The claim describes the study's methodology and is supported by data generated in the study.

claim: Most of the mosquito species in the study are associated with vector activity for various pathogens in their respective ecologies.
source: Most of these species are associated with vector activity for various pathogens in their respective ecologies (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by information presented in Table 1.

claim: The study sequenced the mitochondrial COI gene to perform molecular species identification of samples and to comparatively evaluate the use of rRNA as a molecular marker.
source: In parallel, we sequenced the mitochondrial COI gene to perform molecular species identification of our samples and to comparatively evaluate the use of rRNA as a molecular marker (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim describes the study's methodology as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Depletion efficiency decreases with taxonomic distance from Ae. aegypti.
source: Depletion efficiency decreases with taxonomic distance from Ae. aegypti underlining the need for reference sequences for species of interest.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Total RNA samples contain rRNA from other organisms associated with the host (microbiota, external parasites, or ingested diet) in addition to host rRNA.
source: Apart from host rRNA, total RNA samples also contain rRNA from other organisms associated with the host (microbiota, external parasites, or ingested diet).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the composition of total RNA samples.

claim: rRNA sequences share high homology in conserved regions.
source: As rRNA sequences share high homology in conserved regions, Illumina reads (150 bp) from non-host rRNA can interfere with the contig assembly of host 28S and 18S rRNA.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about rRNA sequence conservation.

claim: Illumina reads (150 bp) from non-host rRNA can interfere with the contig assembly of host 28S and 18S rRNA.
source: As rRNA sequences share high homology in conserved regions, Illumina reads (150 bp) from non-host rRNA can interfere with the contig assembly of host 28S and 18S rRNA.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the high homology of rRNA sequences.

claim: The score-based filtration strategy allowed bioinformatic removal of interfering rRNA reads and achieved successful de novo assembly of 28S and 18S rRNA sequences for all specimens.
source: Our score-based filtration strategy, described in detail in the Materials and methods section, allowed us to bioinformatically remove interfering rRNA reads and achieve successful de novo assembly of 28S and 18S rRNA sequences for all our specimens.
evidence: The claim is supported by data generated in the study.

claim: For each Illumina read, a ratio of BLAST scores against an Insecta library over scores against a Non-Insecta library was computed.
source: Briefly, for each Illumina read, we computed a ratio of BLAST scores against an Insecta library over scores against a Non-Insecta library (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim describes the study's methodology as shown in Figure 2A.

claim: By applying a conservative threshold at 0.8, reads that likely do not originate from mosquito rRNA were removed.
source: By applying a conservative threshold at 0.8 to account for the non-exhaustiveness of the SILVA database, we removed reads that likely do not originate from mosquito rRNA.
evidence: The claim describes the study's methodology.

claim: 15 of the specimens were engorged with vertebrate blood, a rich source of non-mosquito rRNA.
source: Notably, 15 of our specimens were engorged with vertebrate blood, a rich source of non-mosquito rRNA (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Appendix 1—table 1.

claim: The successful assembly of complete 28S and 18S rRNA sequences for specimens engorged with vertebrate blood demonstrates that the filtration strategy performs as expected even with high amounts of non-host rRNA reads.
source: The successful assembly of complete 28S and 18S rRNA sequences for these specimens demonstrates that this strategy performs as expected even with high amounts of non-host rRNA reads.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the successful assembly of rRNA sequences from blood-fed specimens.

claim: For three specimens morphologically identified as Mansonia africana (Specimen ID S33–S35), COI amplification by PCR did not produce any product.
source: We encountered challenges for three specimens morphologically identified as Mansonia africana (Specimen ID S33–S35) (Appendix 1—table 1). COI amplification by PCR did not produce any product, hence COI sequencing could not be used to confirm species identity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The genome assembler SPAdes was only able to assemble partial length rRNA contigs for specimens S33–S35, despite the high number of reads with high scores against the Insecta library.
source: In addition, the genome assembler SPAdes (Bankevich et al., 2012) was only able to assemble partial length rRNA contigs, despite the high number of reads with high scores against the Insecta library.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Guided assembly using the 28S and 18S sequences of 'Ma uniformis CF S51' as references successfully produced full-length contigs for specimens S33–S35.
source: We then performed a guided assembly using the 28S and 18S sequences of this specimen as references, which successfully produced full-length contigs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: In two specimens (Specimen ID S34 and S35), the assembly initially produced two sets of 28S and 18S rRNA sequences, one similar to mosquito rRNA with low coverage and another with 10-fold higher coverage and 95% nucleotide sequence similarity to a water mite of genus Horreolanus.
source: In two of these specimens (Specimen ID S34 and S35), our assembly initially produced two sets of 28S and 18S rRNA sequences, one of which was similar to mosquito rRNA with low coverage and another with 10-fold higher coverage and 95% nucleotide sequence similarity to a water mite of genus Horreolanus known to parasitize mosquitoes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The study assembled 122 28S and 114 18S full-length rRNA sequences for 33 mosquito species representing 10 genera sampled from four countries across three continents.
source: Altogether, we were able to assemble 122 28S and 114 18S full-length rRNA sequences for 33 mosquito species representing 10 genera sampled from four countries across three continents.
evidence: The claim is supported by data generated in the study.

claim: The dataset contains the first records for 30 mosquito species and for seven genera: Coquillettidia, Mansonia, Limatus, Mimomyia, Uranotaenia, Psorophora, and Eretmapodites.
source: This dataset contains, to our knowledge, the first records for 30 mosquito species and for seven genera: Coquillettidia, Mansonia, Limatus, Mimomyia, Uranotaenia, Psorophora, and Eretmapodites.
evidence: The claim is supported by data generated in the study and comparison with existing databases.

claim: The 28S rRNA sequences generally clustered according to their respective species and subgenera, supported by moderate to good bootstrap support at terminal nodes.
source: Although we rarely found records for the same species included in our study, the resulting tree showed that our 28S sequences generally clustered according to their respective species and subgenera, supported by moderate to good bootstrap support at terminal nodes.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Species taxa generally formed monophyletic clades, with the exception of An. gambiae and Cx. quinquefasciatus.
source: Species taxa generally formed monophyletic clades, with the exception of An. gambiae and Cx. quinquefasciatus.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 3.

claim: An. gambiae 28S rRNA sequences formed a clade with closely related sequences from Anopheles arabiensis, Anopheles merus, and Anopheles coluzzii, suggesting unusually high interspecies homology for Anophelines or other members of subgenus Cellia.
source: An. gambiae 28S rRNA sequences formed a clade with closely related sequences from Anopheles arabiensis, Anopheles merus, and Anopheles coluzzii, suggesting unusually high interspecies homology for Anophelines or other members of subgenus Cellia (Figure 3, in purple, subgenus Cellia).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Cx. quinquefasciatus 28S rRNA sequences formed a taxon paraphyletic to sister species Culex pipiens.
source: Meanwhile, Cx. quinquefasciatus 28S rRNA sequences formed a taxon paraphyletic to sister species Culex pipiens (Figure 3, in coral, subgenus Culex).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 3.

claim: 28S rRNA sequence-based phylogenetic reconstructions showed marked incongruence to that of 18S rRNA sequences.
source: 28S rRNA sequence-based phylogenetic reconstructions (Figure 3, with GenBank sequences; Figure 4—figure supplement 1, this study only) showed marked incongruence to that of 18S rRNA sequences (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of phylogenetic trees in Figures 3, 4—figure supplement 1, and 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: All rRNA trees show the bifurcation of family Culicidae into subfamilies Anophelinae (genus Anopheles) and Culicinae (all other genera).
source: Although all rRNA trees show the bifurcation of family Culicidae into subfamilies Anophelinae (genus Anopheles, in purple) and Culicinae (all other genera), the recovered intergeneric phylogenetic relationships vary between the 28S and 18S rRNA trees and are weakly supported.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The 18S rRNA tree exhibited several taxonomic anomalies including the lack of definitive clustering by species within the Culex subgenus, the lack of distinction between 18S rRNA sequences of Cx. pseudovishnui and Cx. tritaeniorhynchus, the placement of Ma sp.3 CF S35 within a Culex clade, and the lack of a monophyletic Mimomyia clade.
source: The 18S rRNA tree also exhibited several taxonomic anomalies: (i) the lack of definitive clustering by species within the Culex subgenus (in coral); (ii) the lack of distinction between 18S rRNA sequences of Cx. pseudovishnui and Cx. tritaeniorhynchus (in coral); (iii) the placement of Ma sp.3 CF S35 (in dark green) within a Culex clade; and (iv) the lack of a monophyletic Mimomyia clade (in teal) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: 28S and 18S rRNA sequences are encoded by linked loci in rDNA clusters and should not be analysed separately.
source: However, 28S and 18S rRNA sequences are encoded by linked loci in rDNA clusters and should not be analysed separately.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about rRNA gene organization.

claim: When concatenated 28S+18S rRNA sequences were generated from the same specimens, the phylogenetic tree resulting from these sequences more closely resembles the 28S tree with regard to the basal position of the Mimomyia clade within the Culicinae subfamily with good bootstrap support.
source: Indeed, when concatenated 28S+18S rRNA sequences were generated from the same specimens (Figure 4), the phylogenetic tree resulting from these sequences more closely resembles the 28S tree (Figure 3) with regard to the basal position of the Mimomyia clade (in teal) within the Culicinae subfamily with good bootstrap support in either tree (84% in 28S rRNA tree, 100% in concatenated 28S+18S rRNA tree).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: For internal nodes, bootstrap support values were higher in the concatenated tree compared to the 28S tree.
source: For internal nodes, bootstrap support values were higher in the concatenated tree compared to the 28S tree.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data comparing Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The 28S+18S rRNA tree formed an Aedini tribe-clade encompassing taxa from genera Psorophora, Aedes, and Eretmapodites, possibly driven by the inclusion of 18S rRNA sequences.
source: Interestingly, the 28S+18S rRNA tree formed an Aedini tribe-clade encompassing taxa from genera Psorophora (in yellow), Aedes (in dark blue), and Eretmapodites (in brown), possibly driven by the inclusion of 18S rRNA sequences.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Concatenation resolved the anomalies found in the 18S rRNA tree and added clarity to the close relationship between Culex and Mansonia taxa.
source: Concatenation also resolved the anomalies found in the 18S rRNA tree and added clarity to the close relationship between Culex (in coral) and Mansonia (in dark green) taxa.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of phylogenetic trees in Figures 4 and 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Relative to the 28S tree, the Culex and Mansonia genera are no longer monophyletic in the concatenated 28S+18S rRNA tree.
source: Of note, relative to the 28S tree (Figure 3) the Culex and Mansonia genera are no longer monophyletic in the concatenated 28S+18S rRNA tree (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of phylogenetic trees in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Genus Culex is paraphyletic with respect to subgenus Mansonoides of genus Mansonia.
source: Genus Culex is paraphyletic with respect to subgenus Mansonoides of genus Mansonia (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Ma. titillans and Ma sp.4 always formed a distinct branch in 28S or 18S rRNA phylogenies, thus possibly representing a clade of subgenus Mansonia.
source: Ma. titillans and Ma sp.4, which we suspect to be Mansonia pseudotitillans, always formed a distinct branch in 28S or 18S rRNA phylogenies, thus possibly representing a clade of subgenus Mansonia.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis data.

claim: The concatenated 28S+18S rRNA tree recapitulates the early divergence of subfamily Anophelinae from subfamily Culicinae.
source: The concatenated 28S+18S rRNA tree (Figure 4) recapitulates what is classically known about the systematics of our specimens, namely (i) the early divergence of subfamily Anophelinae from subfamily Culicinae, (ii) the division of genus Anopheles (in purple) into two subgenera, Anopheles and Cellia, (iii) the division of genus Aedes (in dark blue) into subgenera Stegomyia and Ochlerotatus, (iv) the divergence of the monophyletic subgenus Melanoconion within the Culex genus (in coral) (Harbach, 2007; Harbach and Kitching, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 4 and citations to Harbach, 2007 and Harbach and Kitching, 2016.

claim: The concatenated 28S+18S rRNA tree recapitulates the division of genus Anopheles into two subgenera, Anopheles and Cellia.
source: The concatenated 28S+18S rRNA tree (Figure 4) recapitulates what is classically known about the systematics of our specimens, namely (i) the early divergence of subfamily Anophelinae from subfamily Culicinae, (ii) the division of genus Anopheles (in purple) into two subgenera, Anopheles and Cellia, (iii) the division of genus Aedes (in dark blue) into subgenera Stegomyia and Ochlerotatus, (iv) the divergence of the monophyletic subgenus Melanoconion within the Culex genus (in coral) (Harbach, 2007; Harbach and Kitching, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 4 and citations to Harbach, 2007 and Harbach and Kitching, 2016.

claim: The concatenated 28S+18S rRNA tree recapitulates the division of genus Aedes into subgenera Stegomyia and Ochlerotatus.
source: The concatenated 28S+18S rRNA tree (Figure 4) recapitulates what is classically known about the systematics of our specimens, namely (i) the early divergence of subfamily Anophelinae from subfamily Culicinae, (ii) the division of genus Anopheles (in purple) into two subgenera, Anopheles and Cellia, (iii) the division of genus Aedes (in dark blue) into subgenera Stegomyia and Ochlerotatus, (iv) the divergence of the monophyletic subgenus Melanoconion within the Culex genus (in coral) (Harbach, 2007; Harbach and Kitching, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 4 and citations to Harbach, 2007 and Harbach and Kitching, 2016.

claim: The concatenated 28S+18S rRNA tree recapitulates the divergence of the monophyletic subgenus Melanoconion within the Culex genus.
source: The concatenated 28S+18S rRNA tree (Figure 4) recapitulates what is classically known about the systematics of our specimens, namely (i) the early divergence of subfamily Anophelinae from subfamily Culicinae, (ii) the division of genus Anopheles (in purple) into two subgenera, Anopheles and Cellia, (iii) the division of genus Aedes (in dark blue) into subgenera Stegomyia and Ochlerotatus, (iv) the divergence of the monophyletic subgenus Melanoconion within the Culex genus (in coral) (Harbach, 2007; Harbach and Kitching, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 4 and citations to Harbach, 2007 and Harbach and Kitching, 2016.

claim: COI sequences were able to unequivocally determine the species identity in most specimens except for specific cases.
source: COI sequences were able to unequivocally determine the species identity in most specimens except for the following cases.
evidence: The claim is supported by COI sequencing data from the study.

claim: An. coustani COI sequences from the study, regardless of specimen origin, shared remarkably high nucleotide similarity (>98%) with several other Anopheles species such as An. rhodesiensis, An. rufipes, An. ziemanni, An. tenebrosus, although An. coustani remained the most frequent and closest match.
source: An. coustani COI sequences from our study, regardless of specimen origin, shared remarkably high nucleotide similarity (>98%) with several other Anopheles species such as An. rhodesiensis, An. rufipes, An. ziemanni, An. tenebrosus, although An. coustani remained the most frequent and closest match.
evidence: The claim is supported by COI sequencing data from the study.

claim: Three specimens morphologically identified as Ae. opok had COI sequences showing 97–100% similarity to that of Ae. simpsoni.
source: In the case of Ae. simpsoni, three specimens had been morphologically identified as Ae. opok although their COI sequences showed 97–100% similarity to that of Ae. simpsoni.
evidence: The claim is supported by COI sequencing data from the study.

claim: The putative Ae. simpsoni COI sequences shared only 90% and 89% similarity with Ae. luteocephalus and Ae. africanus, respectively, leading to the conclusion that these specimens are Ae. simpsoni.
source: As GenBank held no records of Ae. opok COI at the time of this study, we instead aligned the putative Ae. simpsoni COI sequences against two sister species of Ae. opok: Ae. luteocephalus and Ae. africanus. We found they shared only 90% and 89% similarity, respectively. Given this significant divergence, we concluded these specimens to be Ae. simpsoni.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on COI sequencing data from the study.

claim: Ambiguous COI results were especially frequent among Culex specimens belonging to the Cx. pipiens or Cx. vishnui subgroups, where the query sequence differed with either of the top two hits by a single nucleotide.
source: Ambiguous results were especially frequent among Culex specimens belonging to the Cx. pipiens or Cx. vishnui subgroups, where the query sequence differed with either of the top two hits by a single nucleotide.
evidence: The claim is supported by COI sequencing data from the study.

claim: Two of three Ma. titillans specimens appeared to belong to a single species that is different from but closely related to Ma. titillans, surmised to be Ma. pseudotitillans based on morphological similarity.
source: Among our three specimens of Ma. titillans, two appeared to belong to a single species that is different from but closely related to Ma. titillans. We surmised that these specimens could instead be Ma. pseudotitillans based on morphological similarity but were not able to verify this by molecular means as no COI reference sequence is available for this species.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on COI sequencing data and morphological observations.
